Gold Catalysis
Gold-Catalyzed Sequential Cycloisomerization of 1,3,9-Ene-
allene-ynes to Fused Spirocarbocycles
Xianxiao Chen, [a][‡] Xiangxiang Ling, [a][‡] Di An, [a] and Weidong Rao* [a]
Abstract: An efficient synthetic method to prepare architectur-
ally challenging spiro tetrahydro-3 H-dicyclopenta[a,b]naphth-
alene derivatives from Au(I)-catalyzed intramolecular sequential
cycloisomerization of linear 1,3,9-ene-allene-ynes is described.
Introduction
Fused spriocarbocycles are common structural motifs found in
a diverse range of bioactive terpenoid natural products and
pharmaceuticals.
[1–7] For instance, conidigenone, [2] conidi-
genone C, [3] waihoensene,[4] phomopsene,[5] lycojaponicumin
C[6] and roquefornine A, [7] all feature 6–5–5 fused spiro-tricyclic
carbocycle skeletons (Figure 1). Moreover, they also serve as
versatile synthetic precursors for the synthesis of structurally
complex natural products.
[8] Accordingly, the development of
new and efficient synthetic strate gies for their efficient con-
struction from readily acc essible substrates w ould be highly de-
sirable.
Figure 1. Selected examples of natural products containing the 6–5–5 fused
spiro-tricyclic carbocycle skeletons.

The proposed cycloisomerization pathway involves an initial
gold-catalyzed 1,3-ene-allene cycloisomerization, followed by a
formal [4+2] cycloaddition to give fused spirocarbocyclic prod-
ucts containing a quaternary centre.
Recently, gold-catalyzed cycloisomerization of enynes, ene-
allenes and allene-alkynes have emerged as one of the most
powerful and versatile synthetic strategies for the efficient and
atom-economical assembly of various carbo- and heterocycles
from readily accessible substrates in a single operation.
[9–11]
However, the analogous cascade reactions of starting materials
containing an alkene, allene and alkyne motif, such as 1,n,m-
ene-allene-ynes, have been rarely explored.
[12,13] The explora-
tion into these reactions has been limited, so far, their in situ
generation as reactive intermediates from Au(I)-catalyzed tan-
dem 1,3-acyloxy migration/cycloisomerization of 1-ene-n,m-di-
yne esters.
[14] To the best of our knowledge, only two reports
have so far been developed on the exploration of the reactivi-
ties of preformed 1,n,m-ene-allene-ynes in gold catalysis, as
shown in Scheme 1.
[13] For example, Liu and co-workers dis-
closed that 1,3,8-ene-allene-ynes could proceed efficiently in
the presence of gold catalyst to form bicyclo[4.3.0]nonadiene
derivatives through 6-endo-dig/Nazarov cyclization cascade
(Scheme 1a).
[13a] Very recently, we developed an efficient syn-
thetic protocol to prepare cycloalkyl- and (hetero)aryl-fused bi-
cyclo[3.3.1]nonane derivatives that relied on gold(I)-catalyzed
cyclopropanation/[5+3] cycloaddition of 1,4,9- and 1,4,10-
allenenynes (Scheme 1b).
[13b]
In 2007, two novel and efficient synthetic approaches that
relied on gold(I) and PtCl 2-catalyzed cycloisomerizations of 1,3-
ene-allenes leading to highly functionalized cyclopentadienes
were reported independently by Toste
[15a] and Iwasawa [15b]
(Scheme 1c). In addition, Echavarren and co-workers developed
a novel gold(I)-catalyzed intramolecular [4+2] cycloaddition
of 1,6-arylalkyne-alkenes which provided rapid access to
2,3,9,9a-tetrahydro-1H-cyclopenta[b]naphthalene derivatives
(Scheme 1d).
[16] Inspired by these pioneer works and as part of
ongoing efforts in the field of gold catalysis, [13b,14] we became
interested in the potential reactivity of preformed 1,3,9-ene-
allene-ynes, the chemistry of which has so far remained unex-
plored. We envisioned that a gold(I)-cascade process involving
an initial 1,3-ene-allene cycloisomerization followed by a formal
[4+2] cycloaddition
[17] might be feasible using 1,3,9-ene-allene-
ynes. Herein, we describe the details of this chemistry that pro-

1,n,m-ene-allene-ynes and pioneer work involving 1,3-allene-enes and 1,6-
ene-arylalkynes.
vides an expedient and chemoselective approach to access an
architecturally challenging class of spiro tetrahydro- 3H-dicyclo-
penta[a,b]naphthalene frameworks containing an all carbon
quaternary centre from all-carbon tethered linear 1,3,9-ene-
allene-ynes.
Results and Discussion
Our studies commenced by examining the gold(I)-catalyzed se-
quential cycloisomerization of 1,3,9-ene-allene-yne 1a to estab-
lish the optimum reaction conditions (Table 1). This initially re-
vealed that treating 1a with 5 mol-% of gold(I) phosphine cata-
lyst A in DCE at room temperature for 12 h afforded the sprio
tetrahydro-3H-dicyclopenta[a,b]naphthalene 2a in 86 % yield
(entry 1). The structure of 2a was unambiguously ascertained
by X-ray crystallographic analysis of a closely related analogue
(vide infra).
[18] A similar outcome was observed upon changing
catalyst from A to more sterically crowded Au(I) complex B or
NHC-gold(I) ( NHC = N-heterocyclic carbene) complexes C-D
with C providing the highest yield of 90 % (entries 2–4). How-
ever, no reaction was detected by TLC and 1H NMR measure-
ments when Ph3PAuNTf2 was used (entry 5). Switching the reac-
tion solvent from DCE to PhMe resulted in a slightly lower yield
Eur. J. Org. Chem. 2020, 5227–5233 www.eurjoc.org © 2020 Wiley-VCH GmbH5228
of 2a (entry 6). However, no reaction was observed for reactions
using THF or MeCN as solvents (entries 7–8). Therefore, reaction
of 1a in the presence of gold catalyst C (5 mol-%) in DCE at
room temperature for 12 h provided the optimum reaction con-
ditions.

[c] No reaction based on TLC analysis and
1H NMR measurements of the
crude reaction mixture.
With the optimized conditions in hand, we next examined
the scope and generality of the present procedure with a vari-
ety of 1,3,9-ene-allene-ynes, and the results are outlined in
Scheme 2. Overall, the NHC-gold(I) complex C-catalyzed reac-
tion conditions proved to be broad, producing a diverse array
of sprio tetrahydro- 3H-dicyclopenta[a,b]naphthalenes contain-
ing a variety of substitution patterns in 60–96 % yields. Reac-
tions of substrates containing a var iety of functional groups,
such as esters ( 1b–c), ether ( 1d), sulfonamide ( 1e), phthalimide
(1f ) on the alkenyl side chain we re well-tolerated, furnishing
the corresponding products 2b–f in excellent yields. Similarly,
substrates possessing either linear ( 1g–i) or cyclic alkyl groups
such as cyclohexyl ( 1j) at the R
1 position all proceed smoothly
under the optimal conditions and led to the formation of the
desired products 2g–j in 81–90 % yields. Subsequently, sub-
strates with a pendant aryl acetylenic motif containing different
substituents, such as sulfonamide ( 1k–m), aryl ( 1n–o) at the
para-position or methyl ( 1q) at the ortho-position of the benz-
ene ring were found to be amenable, providing the desired
products 2k–o and 2q in good yields (70–83 %) with the struc-
ture of 2o unambiguously confirmed by X-ray crystallographic
analysis.
[18] However, a slightly lower yield of 62 % was ob-
served when the substrate 1p containing a strong electron-
withdrawing CF3 group at the para-position of the phenyl moi-
ety was subjected to the optimized conditions. Notably, sub-
strate 1r with a meta-methyl phenyl at the alkyne terminus pro-
vided the desired product 2r in 77 % yield as an inseparable

doi.org/10.1002/ejoc.202000851
EurJOC
European Journal of Organic Chemistry
mixture of regioisomers in a ratio of 10:1. Intriguingly, we found
that the reactions of 1,3,9-ene-allene-ynes bearing a pendant
heteroaryl moiety at the alkyne terminus, such as indole ( 1t)
and thiophene ( 1u), proceeded efficiently to produce the corre-
sponding products 2t–u in 66–76 % yields. Significantly, se-
quential cycloisomerization of substrates incorporating disub-
stituted alkenes ( 1v–w) was also compatible, affording tetra-
hydro-3H-dicyclopenta[a,b] naphthalenes 2v–w in good yields,
albeit as inseparable mixtures of diastereomers in 2.6:1 and
6.1:1 ratios for 2v and 2w, respectively. Gratifyingly, the starting
material that bears a trisubstituted allenyl motif ( 1x) also pro-
ceeded well to provide the corresponding product 2x in 64 %
yield.
Scheme 2. Subst rate scope of 1,3,9-ene-allene-ynes. Reaction conditions: 1
(0.3 mol) and gold complex C (5 mol-%) in DCE (3 mL) at room temperature
for 12–24 h; isolated yields.
To further demonstrate the scalability and practicality of the
present protocol, a scale-up reaction of 1e (2.1 mmol, 1.04 g)
was carried out using only 2 mol-% gold(I) catalyst C under
the optimized conditions, affording the desired product 2e in
excellent yield of 88 % (Scheme 3). Subjecting compound 2e to
m-CPBA in DCE at room temperature for 24 h provided the
diepoxide product 3e in 88 % yield as a single diastereomer.
Eur. J. Org. Chem. 2020, 5227–5233 www.eurjoc.org © 2020 Wiley-VCH GmbH5229
Subsequently, treatment of 3e with FeCl 3 in DCE at 80 °C for
2 h furnished the diketone 4e in 68 % yield.
Scheme 3. Gram-scale synthesis and synthetic transformations.
Several control experiments were performed to gain further
insight into the reaction mechanism (Scheme 4). First, to isolate
a possible intermediate, substrate 1y that bears a 2,6-dimethyl-
phenyl motif at the alkyne terminus was subjected to the opti-
mized reaction conditions (Scheme 4a). Unfortunately, the cy-
clopentadiene product was not isolable due to rapid polymeri-
zation upon treating with column chromatography. Gratifyingly,
repeating the reaction for 1 h followed by the addition of
N-phenylmaleimide for an additional 15 hours produced the
[4+2] adduct 6 in 81 % yield (Scheme 4b).
[19] These results indi-
cated that the cyclopentadiene species was involved as the key
intermediate.
Scheme 4. Control experiments.
On the basis of the above observations and literature re-
ports,[15,16] a plausible mechanism for the present Au(I)-cata-
lyzed sequential cycloisomerization reaction is proposed, as il-
lustrated in Scheme 5. Using 1a as a representative example,
this might initially involve selective activation of the allene
moiety of the substrate by the gold(I) complex to give the gold-
coordinated 1,3,9-ene-allene-yne species Ia. This may then lead
to a Nazarov cyclization of Ia via the pentadienyl cation IIa to
give the cationic intermediate species IIIa or its resonance form

Full Paper
doi.org/10.1002/ejoc.202000851
EurJOC
European Journal of Organic Chemistry
gold carbenoid species IIIa′, followed by 1,2-hydride migration
and deauration to produce the cyclopentadiene intermediate
IVa and regenerate the gold(I) catalyst.
[11a,15] Further activation
of the remaining pendant alkyne moiety by the gold(I) complex
would result in either a step-wise or concerted formal [4+2]
cycloaddition
[16,17] to deliver the Wheland intermediate VIIa,
which upon rearomatization followed by protondeauration,
yields the final product 2a and regenerates the gold(I) catalyst.
Scheme 5. Proposed mechanism for gold(I)-catalyzed sequential cycloisomer-
ization of 1,3,9-ene-allene-ynes represented by 1a.
Conclusion
In summary, we have developed an efficient strategy for the
synthesis of spiro tetrahydro- 3H-dicyclopenta[a,b] naphthalenes
from gold catalyzed sequential cycloisomerization of 1,3,9-ene-
allene-ynes. The transformation has excellent functional group
tolerance and provided the corresponding products in good to
excellent yields under mild conditions. The synthetic utility of
the present method was also demonstrated by the scale-up
preparation of one example followed by its conversion to the
corresponding dioxides and diketones. Efforts to explore the
synthetic applications of the present reactions are currently un-
derway and will be reported in due course.
Experimental Section
To a solution of 1,3,9-ene-allene-yne 1 (0.3 mmol) in DCE (3 mL)
was added gold(I) complex C (14 mg, 15 μmol, 5 mol-%) and the
reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 12 h. Upon
completion, the solvent was removed under reduced pressure and
the residue was purified by flash column chromatography on silica
gel (eluent: petroleum ether/Et
2O = 100:1 to 10:1) to give the de-
sired product 2 in 60–96 % yields.
